title: Surdas
hook: a small boy with butter on his face makes his case

segments.voice: Yesterday, Surdas turned from his own sorrow to a little boy asking when his braid would grow. Who did you turn toward? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

The complaint comes from the neighbors. Butter is missing from their houses again. Pots are cracked. There are small handprints. So the accused is brought before his mother, and the song lets us see his face, which still has a shine of butter on it. He doesn't cry. He doesn't run. He opens his mouth and begins his defense. This is one of the songs carried under the name of Surdas, and it plays like a tiny courtroom: one small boy, no lawyer, and an argument he has clearly been working on.
screen: `THE NEIGHBORS COMPLAIN.` → `BUTTER ON HIS FACE.` → `THE DEFENSE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: It opens with the line the whole song hangs on. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the case, point by point. First: at dawn you sent me off behind the cows, and I wandered the forest all day. When would I have had time? Second: look at these arms. I'm a child. How could I reach a pot hung up high? Third: the cowherd boys have it in for me. They smeared it on my face themselves. Then he changes tactics and gets hurt. Mother, you're too trusting, you believe whatever they say. Maybe you think I'm somebody else's child. And then the big finish: here, take back my stick and my blanket. I quit. You've made me dance enough. And the song ends: Surdas says, then Yashoda smiled, and pulled him close against her heart. Case closed. The butter never comes up again. Why would a devotional poet spend a whole song on a child's fib? Earlier this year we heard the Bhagavata tell how the butter thief stole. Surdas adds the defense, and gives the last word to a mother's smile. Her love doesn't wait for the verdict. It doesn't need him to be innocent. And notice whose name sits in the last line. The singer writes himself into the yard, standing there as a witness, watching Yashoda laugh. For a singer the tradition remembers as blind, it's a striking place to stand: the one who sees the moment the scolding turns into a hug.
screen: `MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.` · `DAWN, SMALL ARMS, JEALOUS FRIENDS.` · `TAKE BACK MY STICK. I QUIT.` · then, large: `YASHODA SMILED AND PULLED HIM CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind someone who gets things wrong around you and argues their way out of it: a child, a coworker, a friend, maybe you. Hear the defense the way Yashoda hears it, every point lined up, a little dramatic. Then, instead of ruling on it, picture smiling and opening your arms. You don't have to agree with the argument. Just let the warmth arrive before the verdict, and rest there. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Surdas. The singer who let a small boy argue his case, and gave the last line to his mother's smile.
Your line: warmth before the verdict. Today, when someone hands you their case for why it wasn't their fault, let your warmth arrive before your verdict. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo is sung as a bhajan in homes and temples, and around Krishna's birthday, Janmashtami, children sometimes act out the butter thief's story.

fork.setup: you're small, there's butter on your face, and your mother is waiting with the neighbors' complaint. what do you do?
options: argue: the cows at dawn, my small arms, my jealous friends.
run off to the forest until it blows over.
fork.reveal: he argues, point by point, then gets hurt and offers to quit. and it works, though not on the evidence: Yashoda smiles and hugs him.

original.note: Hindi and Braj, in Devanagari: butter, the fresh churned kind he is accused of stealing.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute song about a naughty child.
what it means: a mother's love that arrives before the verdict.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata tells the stealing; this pada adds the boy's defense, and the singer's own name in the last line puts him in the yard as a witness.
recall: watching until the dust is gone
